title: Quick and accurate identification of triggerfishes (Balistidae) using PCR with species-diagnostic mitochondrial (12S/16S) primers

authors.affiliation: Nova Southeastern University, Oceanographic Center, 8000 Ocean Drive, Dania, FL 33004 USA

abstract_text: Identification of ichthyoplankton (eggs, larvae, and juveniles) can be a challenging task due to their small sizes and dynamic development. This problem is particularly acute for tropical and subtropical ichthyoplankton, most of which can be identified to family-level only. As part of a broader initiative to develop molecular markers for tropical and subtropical fish identification, we report on the utility of mitochondrial ribosomal gene sequences for triggerfish species identification. A 1,510 bp fragment, containing portions of the mitochondrial ribosomal genes (12S, 16S) and the complete tRNA valine gene, was sequenced from six triggerfish species (4 genera) inhabiting the western central Atlantic Ocean. Forty-three sequences were examined to assess intra- and interspecific variation. Intraspecific differences were minor (less than 0.5%); however, sufficient interspecific differences occur within this locus to allow the design of robust species-specific PCR primers. When tested in a multiplex PCR assay, these primers yielded species-diagnostic size fragments that unambiguously identified all 4 genera and 4 of the 6 species. Distinction between the two Canthidermis congeners (0.9% interspecific variation) was not possible using this approach; however, these congeners were readily distinguished using RFLP analysis of the PCR amplicon. We suggest that molecular genetic approaches can provide a robust and rapid method to tackle long-standing problems in the identification of fish species.

title: Evolution of karyotypes, reproductive organs, and trophic structures in the Goodeidae (Pisces: Cyprinodontiformes) based on nuclear and mitochondrial DNA phylogenies: The continuing saga

authors.affiliation: The University of Alabama, Department of Biological Sciences, Box 870345, Tuscaloosa, Alabama 35487-0345 USA

abstract_text: The family Goodeidae is a distinct North American lineage of freshwater fishes and is comprised of two monophyletic subfamilies (Empetrichthyinae and Goodeinae). Empetrichthyinae contains all egg-laying species and Goodeinae contains all viviparous species. The Goodeinae is recognized as a monophyletic group based on the presence of unique morphological traits associated with internal fertilization and viviparity. The classification of goodeids has been based largely on variation of reproductive and trophic characters. A molecular phylogenetic hypothesis is presented based on the cladistic analysis of mtDNA (portions of the 16s rRNA, control region, and cytochrome b genes) and nDNA (a portion of the tyrosine kinase X-src gene) of representative goodeid fishes. The comparative method based on the molecular phylogeny was used to reconstruct the evolution of key characters traditionally used in the classification of the group such as: trophotaeniae (external projections of the embryonic gut that absorb maternal nutrients), karyotypes, and tooth and jaw structures. The phylogeny agrees with some but not all conclusions from earlier studies regarding phylogenetic relationships and reproductive and trophic character evolution.

title: Are you considering transplantation as a management tool? Be cautious - mixing gene pools may be more harmful than helpful due to outbreeding depression

authors.affiliation: The University of Georgia, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802 USA

abstract_text: Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts inbreeding depression (ID) for offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (i. e., OD occurs). Populations of eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms. OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage sections (7 of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.

title: Evolution of the biomechanical attributes of long bones in fish, amphibians, and reptiles

authors.affiliation: Biomechanical Engineering Division, Mechanical Engineering Department, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305-3030 USA

abstract_text: Long bones are the major skeletal elements of vertebrate appendages. The radiations of many vertebrate clades were facilitated by locomotory innovations involving these elements (e.g. the terrestrial diversification of tetrapods) and thus it is necessary to understand how these elements changed biomechanically to more fully understand vertebrate evolution. Biomechanical attributes of long bones such as strength, modulus, and loading conditions are well documented in avian and mammalian taxa. However, data for taxa from outgroup clades are virtually non-existent and the results from the few studies that have been conducted are not in accord with those obtained for bird and mammal bones. In order to provide a better understanding of skeletal evolution, I conducted a series of biomechanical tests on long bones from a diversity of fish, amphibians, and reptiles that possessed basal locomotory attributes within their respective clades. Evolutionary trends were assessed using phylogenetic character analysis. The results suggest: 1) material properties (strength, modulus, and failure strain) did not vary throughout evolution, 2) in vivo strain regimes increased independently in birds and mammals, 3) the capacity of long bones to functionally adapt is a plesiomorphic osteichthyan trait, and 4) size and shape changes were the primary means by which long bones changed to meet evolutionary locomotory challenges.

title: Comparative locomotor kinematics of three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, and D. sabina)

authors.affiliation: University of Chicago, Dept. OBA, 1027 E. 57th, Chicago, IL 60637, USA

abstract_text: Locomotion in stingrays occurs as waves are propagated along their broadly expanded pectoral fins and can range from being undulatory to oscillatory. This study compares swimming behavior in three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, D. sabina) differing in fin design (disc shape) as measured by aspect ratio (AR). Three-dimensional video recordings captured swimming kinematics over a range of velocities for the three species. Results indicate that D. americana (highest AR) has a significantly lower wing beat frequency and lower number of waves than the other two species. Wing amplitude, as a percentage of wing span, differs significantly in T. lymma (highest) and D. sabina (lowest). The results of frequency and number of waves corroborate previous studies suggesting that higher aspect ratio fins tend to have a lower frequency and lower number of waves than low aspect ratio fins; however, the amplitude data does not fit the prediction of high AR fins having greater amplitude. Overall, D. americana falls more toward the oscillatory end of the continuum and T. lymma falls toward the undulatory end, with D. sabina somewhere in between these two.

title: Light attenuating molecules in the lens of the fish eye

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biological Sciences, Univ. of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA 90089; Section of Vertebrates, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, 900 Exposition Blvd., Los Angeles, CA 90007 USA

abstract_text: The ocular lens of fishes contains mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), which attenuate short wavelengths of light. The causes for the varied distribution of MAAs in the lenses of different fish species are still in question. In this study I examined the lenticular MAA content of 42 flatfish species (order Pleuronectiformes) from nine families to investigate the controlling factors on lens pigmentation and changes in pigmentation during ontogeny. MAAs were actively transported and concentrated by the lens from the surrounding humors in the eye. These MAAs produced two absorbance peaks when analyzed spectrophotometrically, one near 320 nm and another near 360 nm. The relative amounts of different MAAs in the lens was correlated with phylogeny, while the total MAA concentration reflected the depth distribution of each species. Species living in deeper water contained lower concentrations of MAAs. Both the total amount of MAAs and their relative proportions changed during ontogeny. MAAs began accumulating after settlement, and increased in concentration with standard length. The phylogenetic trend in the relative proportion of MAA peaks suggests that lens pigmentation is under genetic control. This control is not exerted by the lens itself, but may occur at the level of food metabolism.

title: The effects of chronic and periodic acute hypoxia on the growth and physiology of juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, Box 7617, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC 27695

abstract_text: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is proving to be one of the most important determinants of juvenile fish growth and survival in our estuaries. Laboratory experiments were conducted to determine the effects of chronic hypoxia and periodic acute hypoxia on the growth, metabolic rate and blood hematocrit of juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma. Fish were maintained in aquaria having constant salinity (15 psu) and temperature (25 °C) and exposed to constant normoxia (6 mg O2 l-1), constant hypoxia (2.75), an intermediate level (4.5), and a diel oscillating treatment (daily mean = 4.5 mg O2 l-1). Results from the blood hematocrit analysis indicate a secondary stress response to the nocturnal hypoxia in the oscillating treatment resulting in increased blood hematocrit levels. Flounder also exhibited limited growth in the low DO treatment (1.9 % Wt d-1, p<0.001) suggesting a species-level limiting oxygen concentration for growth between the low (2.75) and intermediate (4.5) DO levels. Furthermore, fish in the oscillating treatment realized growth similar to the intermediate treatment indicating that daily growth is a function of the daily mean DO concentrations. This hypothesis is supported by the dramatic overcompensation in the afternoon routine respiration rates exhibited by the oscillating treatment. Further work is necessary to address the synergistic effects of temperature and variable DO on the growth and physiology of juvenile estuarine dependent fish.

title: The influence of temperature on the otolith-somatic growth relationship for juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma

authors.affiliation: NCSU, Dept. of Zoology, Box 7617, Raleigh, NC 27695-7617 USA

abstract_text: Temperature effects on the otolith-somatic growth relationship of southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma were determined in order to back-calculate somatic growth rates of wild-caught fish. Laboratory growth experiments were conducted to measure the somatic and otolith growth of juvenile flounder at five temperatures: 17, 20, 25, 30, and 33 °C. To measure growth rates of wild-caught fish, temperatures were continuously monitored and fish were collected in a known flounder nursery area. With slow somatic growth and/or low temperatures (17 and 20 °C), ring counts from laboratory fish were underestimated. Otolith growth (OG) was significantly correlated with temperature (T) and somatic growth (G) with the strongest relationship measured at areas near the sulcus on the right otolith: OG = 0.2352(G) + 0.0481(T) - 0.5842 (R2 = 0.74). Increment counts from fish exposed to 17 and 20 °C were underestimated; therefore, reliable estimates of growth could not be obtained. Therefore, this otolith-somatic growth equation can only be used for temperatures greater than 25 °C. In this case, predicted growth rates were 2.7 - 15.7 % d-1 showing that flounder are not growth limited in North Carolina estuaries.

title: Comparative physiology of metabolic rate and thermal tolerance: physiological parameters for investigating macroecological patterns

authors.affiliation: University of Oklahoma, Dept. of Zoology, Univ. of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73019

abstract_text: Distributional patterns of species result in part from their ability to tolerate physiologically the environmental extremes characteristic within their geographical range. Macroecology attempts to reveal relationships between organisms and their environments by investigating statistical patterns of abundance and distribution. In such analyses, species serve as replicates where the relationship between range and body size is used to understand how physical space and ecological resources are partitioned to create the unique distributions of species. However, these studies often fail to consider the underlying physiological capacities and tolerances that are most likely to be the limiting factors in determining distributions. I measured temperature dependent metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance in several ectothermic species in an attempt to investigate two subsidiary principles of Shelford's law and determine if physiological parameters are better predictors of distributional patterns than are measures of body size. After controls for phylogeny, I found species-specific plasticity of metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance to predict better the statistical patterns of geographic range size and latitudinal range among the fishes and snakes studied. These findings support Shelford's idea that the distributions of species often are governed by the environmental factor for which species have the narrowest tolerance range or least adaptability.

title: Patterns of variation in spring emergence by black rat snakes (Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta)

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, ON, K1S 5B6
Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, ON, K1S 5B6
Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, ON, K1S 5B6

abstract_text: Substantial individual variation in timing of emergence from hibernation has been reported among reptiles, although few studies have addressed the causes of that variation. Here we report patterns of spring emergence by black rat snakes (Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta), observed at 13 communal hibernacula in eastern Ontario from 1992 to 1997. Although we found significant variations in timing of emergence among years and among hibernacula, we found no evidence of a simple latitudinal gradient in mean emergence dates. Within hibernacula, significantly more snakes emerged on days with high maximum air temperatures, but maximum air temperature only explained a small amount of the variation among years in emergence dates. Larger individuals emerged earlier than smaller individuals and females tended to emerge earlier than males. Condition was not a significant factor determining timing of emergence in our black rat snake population. Based on these results, we proposed the preparation for reproduction hypothesis which states that mature individual snakes emerge earlier than immature individuals to prepare their gonads for reproduction.

title: Movement patterns and microhabitat use of the brown tree snake, Boiga irregularis

authors.affiliation: Ohio Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Ohio State University, 1735 Neil Avenue, Columbus OH 43210 USA

abstract_text: The Brown Tree Snake (BTS), Boiga irregularis, is a nocturnal, arboreal species accidentally introduced to the island of Guam, and associated with the loss of most of the island's native forest vertebrates. Little is known about the movement patterns of this species or that of other nocturnal, arboreal snakes. I investigated the overnight spatial movement patterns of BTS using two tracking devices; standard radio telemetry and a quilting cocoon of cotton thread (240 m), which delineated the snake's path. I recorded microhabitat data at every one meter interval along the tracking thread path. Ten BTS were tracked a minimum of 30 meters (mean = 92.9 m). The total distances moved were on average twice the straight-line distance from initial capture/release location to refugium. There was no significant correlation between body size and percentage of movement above ground, mean height above ground, or mean height of forest canopy used. There was a significant positive relationship between mean support diameter and BTS body size (R square = 0.596, P = 0.0148). There was also a significant positive relationship between available forest connectivity and snake pathways. Snakes used certain plants in disproportion to their occurrence in the forest according to relative stability or degree of connectivity.

title: Ecology and habitat use of juvenile box turtles at Egmont Key, Florida

authors.affiliation: Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, 303 Newins-Ziegler Hall, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611 USA

abstract_text: Studies on box turtles (Terrapene carolina baurii) on Egmont Key have been ongoing since 1991. This island off the west coast of Florida is home to more than 2000 turtles. During previous fieldwork, large numbers of juveniles were found. Data on size, habitat, and activity were recorded. Beginning in June 1997, I began an intensive study of juvenile habitat use and movement patterns. Through November, a total of 192 juveniles were located and marked. Thread trailers were attached to 59 juveniles (<121mm) that were tracked until the thread ran out (generally within four days). I recorded canopy cover density and species composition along trails at 10m intervals. Juveniles were found primarily under dense, low ground cover, and frequently travelled at the ecotone between dense canopy and more open areas. Small juveniles (<65mm) were mostly found during the hottest part of the day, and appeared to be basking; at other times, they chose forms under Australian pine needles. Additionally, juvenile habitat use varies with body size. These habitat data can be used to assist in planning island restoration and management.

title: Distribution of the diamondback terrapin, Malaclemys terrapin, in South Carolina salt marshes

authors.affiliation: Graduate Program in Marine Biology, University of Charleston, Grice Marine Biological Laboratory, 205 Fort Johnson Road, Charleston, SC 29412-9110, USA
Graduate Program in Marine Biology, University of Charleston, Grice Marine Biological Laboratory, 205 Fort Johnson Road, Charleston, SC 29412-9110, USA
South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, Marine Resources Division, USA

abstract_text: The diamondback terrapin, Malaclemys terrapin, is the only species of estuarine turtle. The range of Malaclemys extends along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Corpus Christi. Terrapins were nearly hunted to extinction in the early 1900s due to the popularity of terrapin soup. In the years following intense commercial harvest of terrapin, some populations of Malaclemys have recovered. However, although commercial harvesting is no longer a threat to Malaclemys, the stability of terrapin populations is being challenged by incidental drowning in crab traps and habitat destruction. Malaclemys terrapin is frequently caught incidentally in trammel nets used by Inshore Fisheries, South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, Marine Resources Division. Inshore Fisheries has been recording incidental catches of Malaclemys since January 1995. The objective of this study is to determine the distribution of M. terrapin in South Carolina based on incidental catches and physical and geographical data recorded by Inshore Fisheries. The effects explaining most of the variation in terrapin distribution are month and individual location of a sample within one of six major sampling sites. The long-term collection of this data will allow monitoring of Malaclemys populations in regions supporting large crabbing industries and areas undergoing coastal development.

title: Activity and behavior of nesting yellow-blotched map turtles (Graptemys flavimaculata) and their nest predators

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA

abstract_text: Populations of the yellow-blotched map turtle (Graptemys flavimaculata) are known to be declining throughout their limited range. As a result of this decline, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service placed this species on the Federally Endangered Species list in 1991. Low nesting success and high rates of nest depredation are among the contributing factors to this decline, but little is known about nesting behavior and activity or the behaviors of nest predators. We studied nesting behavior, nesting activity, and the behaviors of nest predators of G. flavimaculata on the Pascagoula River in Southeastern Mississippi during 1997. Over 182 hours of observations were made from a blind from 28 May to 13 August. Most nesting attempts occurred between mid May and late July. Nesting was exclusively diurnal; although nesting attempts occurred throughout the day, nesting peaked between 1500-1700 hours. Of the 48 nesting attempts observed, only 11 females completed oviposition. Although the presence of the observer/blind did not significantly affect the completion of oviposition once the female entered the beach, the number of nesting attempts increased when the observer/blind was not present. The only diurnal nest predators observed were fish crows (Corvus ossifragus) and fire ants (Solenopsis invicta). Fish crows were highly aggressive in attacking nests, sometimes driving away nesting females. In six of 21 monitored nests, humans either directly or indirectly influenced nest mortality. Additionally, of the over 78 nests found, only six survived to hatching.

title: Prey preference in neonate brown water snakes, Nerodia taxispilota

authors.affiliation: University of Georgia, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802, USA

abstract_text: I experimentally tested innate prey preference in brown water snakes, Nerodia taxispilota. Nerodia taxispilota is a piscivorous species, and adults consume primarily catfishes (Ictaluridae). Six prey odors (4 fish, 2 amphibians) and a water control were presented on cotton swabs to 13 neonate individuals housed individually in aquaria. Fish odors elicited more tongue flicks than amphibian odors, with catfish (Ictalurus punctatus) odors receiving the most tongue flicks. These results support field results that indicate N. taxispilota prefers fish, especially catfish. Basic foraging ecology and its relationship to recent toxicological studies will also be discussed.

title: Do incubation-induced changes to a lizard's phenotype affect its vulnerability to predators?

authors.affiliation: School of Biological Sciences, University of Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia
School of Biological Sciences, University of Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia

abstract_text: Recent work on a variety of reptiles provides strong evidence that incubation temperatures can influence many aspects of a hatchling's phenotype (i.e., size, shape, activity, locomotor performance, etc.). However, although these traits seem likely to affect the hatchling's fitness, few studies have tested this assumption. Vulnerability to predation is one plausible way that phenotypic modifications could affect an organism's fitness. Therefore, we incubated the eggs of lizards at temperatures similar to the extremes of natural nests, and examined both the response of hatchlings to predator (snake) scent and actual vulnerability in staged encounters in the laboratory. We used two species of montane Australian scincids: one heliotherm (Lampropholis delicata) that deposits eggs in relatively warm nests, and one thigmotherm (Nannoscincus maccoyi) that lays in relatively cool nests. For both species, our results show that incubation temperature affects both an individual's response to predator scent and its vulnerability to predation. These patterns are complex, and change with the age of the hatchling, perhaps through differential growth rates and changes in activity patterns. Nevertheless, these experiments support the notion that incubation-induced modifications to a lizard's phenotype may be biologically significant, and that some of these effects are mediated through predator-prey interactions.

title: Intrapopulational variation in demographic patterns and reproductive traits of gopher frogs (Rana capito) in Mississippi

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana University, Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA

abstract_text: Since 1995, we have been studying the only known population of gopher frogs (Rana capito) in Mississippi to investigate variation in reproductive traits and population demography. Adult size structure, adult survivorship, reproductive success, and juvenile recruitment were monitored through the combination of a complete drift fence and egg mass surveys. There was extensive variation both among and within years in adult traits including intra- and intersexual differences in size, rate of return to the breeding site, survivorship, and breeding-season weight loss. Reproductive success and timing of mortality in eggs and larvae also varied among years. We found no repeatability among years in the relationship between the number of females, egg masses, and emerging juveniles. These data suggest that monitoring through the exclusive use of either egg mass surveys or drift fences may not accurately determine the status of anuran populations. In addition, the wide variation we found among years indicates that short-term studies are inadequate in understanding amphibian population dynamics.

title: Sex and the single female: when do males become unnecessary?

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Palaeobiology, and CBCB, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario, Canada, M5S 2C6

abstract_text: Whiptail lizards of the species genus Cnemidophorus range across the southwestern U.S. into South America. They occupy a variety of habitats and, although they vary in behaviour and ecology, are morphologically conservative. At some point in their evolutionary history, different combinations of species have hybridized to form all-female, self-cloning species. Using information from allozymes, skull morphology, and mitochondrial DNA sequences genes, I am sorting out the evolutionary relationships among North American species of Cnemidophorus to determine: (a) how closely related species have to be to form viable, hybrid unisexuals; (b) whether morphological and ecological similarities among the various species result from common descent or adaptation to similar environments; (c) how and when these lizards speciated and got to where we find them today. Results to date suggest that some of the incredible speciation in Cnemidophorus is due to rapid fragmentation and isolation during the Late Pleistocene, but that some speciation events may have occurred much earlier. This is leading to interesting speculations about the origins of unisexuality in this fascinating group of lizards.

title: Offspring sex ratio variation in northern water snakes, Nerodia sipedon

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, Ontario, K1S 5B6
Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, Ontario, K1S 5B6
Department of Biology, Carleton University, 1125 Colonel By Drive, Ottawa, Ontario, K1S 5B6
Department of Biology, McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario

abstract_text: We used data from 88 litters of northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) to test predictions about how mothers should adaptively vary the sex ratios of their offspring. Sex ratios did not vary with birth date, but larger mothers produced significantly more daughters, and mothers producing larger offspring produced significantly more daughters. Because neonate size did vary with maternal size, the two significant sex ratio patterns were independent of each other. Although these relations provide clear evidence that sex ratios varied non-randomly, only the relation between sex ratio and neonate size was consistent with our predictions if females vary sex ratios adaptively. The limited evidence on neonatal sex ratios for other snake species also indicates variation that is non-random but not necessarily adaptive. Better understanding of these patterns will require information on the factors that differentially affect the fitness of male and female neonates.

title: The reproductive ecology and natural history of the northern leopard frog, Rana pipiens, in a rehabilitated wetland in northeastern Ohio

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, OH 44242
Department of Biological Sciences, Kent State University, Kent, OH 44242

abstract_text: We examined the reproductive ecology and natural history of Rana pipiens in a recently rehabilitated wetland in Barberton, Ohio during the spring and summers of 1996 and 1997. Spawning took place within a three week period beginning in late March when water temperatures exceeded 11 °C. Egg deposition was most concentrated in shallow waters at an average depth of 9 cm. No masses were deposited at depths greater than 20 cm. An estimated 556,000 eggs were deposited by 203 breeding females. 67% of these masses were attached to either emergent, or non-emergent Juncus effusus, Typha angustifolia, or T. latifolia. Juvenile frogs metamorphosed in mid June at an average snout-vent length of 302 mm and a weight of 5.4 g. Mark-recapture analysis revealed a mortality rate suffered between the egg and juvenile stage of over 99%. The stomach contents of 13 adult and 19 juvenile R. pipiens contained invertebrates belonging largely to the insect orders Coleoptera, Hemiptera and Homoptera. Although juvenile frogs consumed more individual prey items than adults (t = 2.196, p<0.05), neither specialized on active or inactive prey (X2 = 3.84, p<0.05). Juvenile frogs in this population failed to reach sexual maturity within their first season of growth.

title: Patterns of frog communities from marshes of the Great Lakes area: a multivariate analysis of habitat and development factors

authors.affiliation: University of Toronto, Zoology Department, Toronto, ON, M5S 3G5

abstract_text: Surveys of calling amphibians in marshes located in Ontario and the Great Lakes' states were conducted by volunteers from April to July in 1995 through the Marsh Monitoring Program. Data from 304 marsh sites were obtained and showed that frog community composition is related to marsh vegetation structure and diversity, surrounding habitat and landuse, and human alterations to marshes. Correspondence analyses showed patterns in frog assemblages that were related to geographic location, species abundance and habitat preferences. One-way ANOVAs of correspondence analysis axes of environmental variables with frog species showed significant differences for some species. These analyses indicate that frog community composition and presence of a species are influenced by the habitat and quality of marshes available in the Great Lakes area.

title: Ecology of an equatorial African leaf-litter herpetofauna, Kibale National Park, Uganda

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, 223 Bartram Hall, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida 32611, USA

abstract_text: Plot sampling was used to compare the wet and dry season litter herpetofaunas of three forest types in Kibale National Park, Uganda. Species richness, abundance, and evenness were measured in pristine, selectively logged, and exotic pine forests. A repeated measures design was also employed to examine whether Ficus natalensis fruiting events influence litter arthropod and herpetofaunal abundances. The diets of the six most common leaf litter anurans were examined to determine important prey-taxa. The richest herpetofaunas were in the pine and logged forests. Lizard richness, abundance, and diversity were greatest in the pine forest. Anuran abundance in the logged forest was double that of the other forests, while diversity was highest in the unlogged forest. The number of herpetofauna in all sites declined during the dry season, with the distribution of captures indicating limited use of hilltops during that season. Relative to Kibale, other tropical wet forests of similar latitude and elevation support a roughly equivalent species richness but at higher densities. This paucity of litter herpetofauna at Kibale does not appear to result from low prey availability, for though the abundance of many prey arthropods increases under fruiting F. natalensis, there is no corresponding increase in herpetofaunal densities.

title: Reptile diversity in a disturbed tropical forest landscape

authors.affiliation: Section of Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
Section of Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
Section of Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA

abstract_text: Throughout the tropics, mature forests are rapidly being replaced with pastures, gardens, and plantations. The goal of this study was to examine the reptile diversity in different agricultural land use regions in and around Los Haitises National Park, Dominican Republic. Transects and trapping grids were used to sample reptiles in nine land use types; active pasture, oil palm and cacao plantations, abandoned pasture, cacao, and conucos (home gardens), and relatively undisturbed forests and karstic hilltops (mogotes). Results indicate that faunal composition varies significantly between land use types. Species richness and abundance per sample were highest on the undisturbed mogotes and lowest in the active pastures. Several rare species of geckos (Sphaerodactylus) were found exclusively on the mogotes. Anolis lizards representing five different ecomorphs were the most abundant lizards in all habitats with each ecomorph being present wherever the appropriate microhabitat was available. Differences in diversity between land use regions were analyzed using ordination plots, diversity indices, and cluster analyses. The results of these analyses suggest that the preservation of undisturbed habitats is critical to the conservation of reptile biodiversity.

title: Cardiac and respiratory rates of juvenile southern stingrays (Dasyatis americana), and the effects of tonic immobility on these systems

authors.affiliation: Millersville University, Millersville, PA; National Aquarium in Baltimore, Baltimore, MD

abstract_text: This study was performed to establish a mean cardiac and respiration rate in juvenile southern stingrays (Dasyatis americana). Thirteen stingrays (23 to 36.6 cm disk width) were used to establish a "normal" cardiac and respiratory rate. The sex, size and individual proved to show no significant change in their respiratory rate. Sex proved not to be significant in relation to their heart rate; yet an allometric relationship was found between their heart rate and body mass. A marginal correlation was found between the cardio-respiratory rates. Further analysis found this relationship to be a function of time; therefore, showing that these systems were out of phase varied between individuals. Tonic immobility (TI) was induced in nine of the juvenile southern stingrays while their cardiac and respiratory rates were monitored. The onset of TI was correlated with a significant decrease from their "normal" cardiac and respiratory rates. The results from the preliminary TI study showed correlations mentioned earlier, including an allometric relationship between heart rate and body size. Therefore, TI causes the cardiac and respiratory rates to slow, ultimately resulting in the animal to exhibit the classic "limp" response.

title: The fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas) in western boreal lakes: Will forest harvesting affect population-level processes?

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada T6G 2E9

abstract_text: Harvesting of Alberta's boreal forest is increasing dramatically. Predicted effects of forest harvesting on lakes in this region involve increases in nutrient loading and primary productivity. Because it is often the most abundant, or only fish present, the fathead is an important component of aquatic food webs in this region. However, little is known about the basic ecology of fathead populations inhabiting these lakes. The objectives of my research are to determine: 1) what factors regulate fathead populations in boreal Alberta lakes; and 2) how potential changes in environmental conditions resulting from forest harvesting may affect these populations. My research is divided into three components: i) the intensive study of four fathead populations before and after experimental forest harvesting; ii) an extensive survey of populations inhabiting lakes throughout the boreal forest of Alberta; and iii) mechanistic pond experiments. Together, these three components should provide important insights into the factors and mechanisms regulating fathead populations, and allow me to assess the effects of forest harvesting on fathead populations in this region.

abstract_text: The short-term, localized nature of grouper spawning aggregations and unequal sex ratios due to protogyny renders many groupers particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure and therefore in need of special management techniques. abstract_text: Research was conducted in the North Fork of the Virgin River within Zion National Park, Utah, USA, to investigate the effects of chronic recreational disturbance on the native fish community. abstract_text: Pacific electric rays were collected from central and southern California from July 1994 through January 1996 for an age and growth, reproduction and demography study. Vertebral centra were used for ageing. The maximum age estimate from vertebral centra was 16 years. The von Bertalanffy growth model provided the best fit to the size at age estimate data, predicting an asymptotic total length (TL) of 1372 mm for females and 921 mm for males. Estimated size (and age) at sexual maturity is 600 mm TL (6 years) for males and 840 mm TL (11 years) in females. Pacific electric rays have a low fecundity of approximately 17 young per litter. Time of parturition could not be determined. Instantaneous mortality estimates (z) ranged from 0.048 to 0.277, depending on the longevity estimates used. Best demographic estimates indicate that the Pacific electric ray population is at or slightly exceeding a stable equilibrium with a generation time of 12.7 to 14.7 years.

abstract_text: The Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Management Division of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is responsible for management of Atlantic tunas, swordfish, billfish and sharks. Thirty-nine species of Atlantic sharks are grouped into 4 management units - large coastal sharks, pelagic sharks, small coastal sharks, and prohibited species. In the 'Report to Congress: Status of the Fisheries of the United States' (September, 1997), NMFS identified all large coastal sharks and prohibited species as overfished, and pelagic and small coastal sharks as fully fished. The Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act of 1996, as amended, requires that all species designated as overfished must have fishery management plans (FMPs) or FMP amendments that include rebuilding plans submitted for Secretarial review within one year (September, 1998) and that NMFS establish an advisory panel for each FMP or amendment. The HMS Management Division is developing a combined HMS plan, with assistance from an HMS Advisory Panel, which will build on the existing plans for sharks and swordfish and will add a new management framework for tunas. An FMP amendment for Atlantic billfish will be prepared separately. An update on the status of the HMS plan will be provided.

abstract_text: This study represents the first experimental trials on an elasmobranch's ability to return home from an unfamiliar area. Ten juvenile lemon sharks (66.0 to 96.0 cm total lengths) were tagged with ultrasonic transmitters and their home ranges determined over a minimum of 3 days of tracking. Thereafter they were recaptured and experimentally displaced 4 km off shore, south of the island. From late October 1997 to February 1998, seven displacements during daylight and three displacements at night were performed. Sharks were tracked for between 2 and 14 hours, and in all ten cases successfully returned to their home ranges. The behavioral pattern of the sharks at the time of release was characterized by circling and vertical migrations suggesting that they were attempting to orient to sensory cues in a way similar to homing pigeons. Further, sharks released at night appeared to change course to a more direct route home at sunrise, suggesting that visual cues may play an important role in the final stages of homing. Therefore, we are testing the hypothesis that sharks are able to use the position of the sun as a cue for orientation. Finally, we are carefully documenting the behavior of sharks at the time of release to give insight into possible mechanisms of orientation. abstract_text: School sharks, Galeorhinus galeus, are an important commercial species in the Australian Southern Shark Fishery. A current project is using archival tags to try and answer certain questions on vertical distribution, 'onshelf' and 'offshelf' movement components, Tasman Sea distribution, pupping migrations and pupping areas. A 'dummy' tagging experiment was carried out to evaluate the suitability of internal versus externally located tags and between unstreamlined and hydrodynamically shaped external tags. The overall recapture rate after three years was 15% and although unstreamlined external tags were returned at a lower rate (11%) than streamlined externals (16%) and internal tags (19%) these differences were not statistically significant. In November 1997, 30 archival tags were deployed on school sharks in waters off South Australia; these tags were mounted externally on the first dorsal fin and were semi-streamlined. One tag was returned after 7 days and another after 23 days. No further returns have been made to date. Both recaptures showed an interesting diurnal vertical migration between as deep as 500 m during the day to near the surface at night. Geo-positioning from the light data are discussed. Immediate plans are to release a further batch of fish with internal tags.

abstract_text: Age and growth of the spiny butterfly ray, Gymnura altavela, was estimated from growth increments visible in the vertebral centra of 175 individuals. Data were comprised of 93 males and 82 females, ranging in size from 250 (embryos) to 2020 mm in disk width. Rays were only collected in August and September (1995-97), thus vertebral increments were assumed to be deposited annually for the purposes of ageing. Vertebral centra were sectioned longitudinally and annuli counted multiple times. Precision of vertebral ageing was estimated using the index of average percent error. Back-calculated size-at-age data were used to estimate von Bertalanffy growth function parameters to describe sex-specific and overall patterns of growth. This study represents a major contribution to general information on this poorly-studied species.

abstract_text: Population growth and exploitation of Alopias superciliosus were estimated by demographic analyses using best known life history parameters. Life history tables were constructed by using both estimates of natural mortality (M) of 0.1316 and age-specific natural mortality for maximum ages of 30. Fecundity was 1 and age at maturity was at age 12. With age-specific mortality, the population increase rate was 1.2%/year, and the generation time was about 16.45 years without exploitation. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the mortality of juvenile stage was the most sensitive factor in input parameters and net reproductive value was the most sensitive factor in computed parameters. abstract_text: A stage-based model of sandbar shark populations indicates that fishing mortality (F) needs to be reduced to 0.08 to ensure sustainability of the population. This model assumes the natural mortality (M) is 0.10. However, stage-based models do not consider the effect size limits may have on the fishery. We have used a yield per recruit (YPR) analysis to examine the effects of adopting different size limits in the fishery. We used various growth parameter estimates, an age of recruitment of 1, and M = 0.10. Based on estimates from Casey et al. (1985), peak YPR occurs at a combination of F = 0.40 and an age of first capture of 10 years or approximately 144 cm fork length (fl). When growth parameter estimates from Casey and Natanson (1992) are used, peak YPR occurs at a combination of F = 0.30 and an age of first capture of 10 years or approximately 99 cm fl. Maximum YPR for F = 0.08, predicted by the stage-based model, is approximately 80% of the peak YPRs found above, and occur at an age of first capture of approximately 6 years. With growth parameters estimated for 1991 to 1992 from Sminkey and Musick (1995), peak YPR occurs at an F = 0.45 and an age of first capture of 9 years or approximately 124 cm fl. In this case, maximum YPR for F = 0.08 is approximately 75% of the peak YPR estimated and occurs at an age of first capture of approximately 5 years. These results suggest that in order to have a stable population, YPR for each set of growth parameter estimates must be 20 to 25% smaller than the peak YPR.

abstract_text: The distribution of basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus) around the Isle of Arran in the Clyde sea area on the west coast of Scotland, UK was investigated during July 1997. A network of shore based volunteers conducted visual searches between 06-00 and 22-00 from seven vantage points for a total of 1538 hours over 20 days between July 6 and 28. Twenty-nine sightings were recorded. A plankton sampling programme was carried out in the same area and over the same time period. The majority of shark sightings occurred in the afternoon and evening corresponding to an increase in zooplankton abundance during this period. Three peaks in shark sightings occurred over the study period which followed peaks in zooplankton abundance with a lag of one to three days. The spatial distribution of shark sightings was also associated with the distribution of zooplankton in the area. Increases in the number of sharks occurred when zooplankton dry weights were at the maximum normally found in the area. This study has shown, therefore, that fine-scale spatio-temporal variability in the distribution of basking sharks can be explained in terms of patchiness in the distribution and abundance of zooplankton.

abstract_text: Young-of-the-year sandbar sharks grow in length before their umbilical scars are healed. This study takes that into account by separating umbilical scar healing stages and produces a more accurate length-at-birth than studies which report the lengths of sandbar sharks with open umbilical scars. We examined 798 sandbar sharks captured by gill net or longline in Delaware Bay between 1995 and 1997. Six distinct umbilical scar healing stages were termed cord-remains, open-fresh, partly-healed, mostly-healed, well-healed and none. Sharks with the three earliest umbilical healing stages did not differ in length, thus represented the length-at-birth. The mean length-at-birth is 49.3 cm ±0.3 cm fork length (95% confidence interval, n=238) with a range of 40 to 55 cm fork length in Delaware Bay. Our results are comparable to published reports of sandbar length-at-birth along the US east coast and therefore do not support the hypothesis that sandbar sharks are born 'somewhat' smaller in the northern pupping range.

abstract_text: The fishery for dogfish (Squalus acanthias) of British Columbia is one of the oldest shark fisheries in the world. This paper describes the main features in the long evolution of this fishery. It also analyses the current situation and the management system of the fishery. Presently, this is a small fishery characterized by strong market limitations. Although there is a reasonably modern management system for the fishery, the apparent success to keep the dogfish stocks at healthy levels for the major part of the 125+ years of the fishery is more a product of the lack of strong demand for dogfish which has offered a fortuitous protection to the stock. Some suggestions for improvements to the stock assessment and possible ways to develop the fishery are given.

abstract_text: Catch volume and trade of the whale shark fishery for the 1997-1998 season was monitored by WWF-Philippines and Silliman University. abstract_text: We describe the shark bycatch in the U.S. gulf menhaden fishery; their species composition, fates, distribution and estimate the annual number of sharks caught by the fishery. Ten species of sharks were identified, with blacktip sharks Carcharhinus limbatus accounting for 50% of those observed. Approximately 75% of the sharks encountered died, 12% were released disoriented and 8% were released healthy. Using loglinear and logit models we determined spatial and temporal patterns in the shark bycatch. Contrasts revealed the odds of observing a fishing set with shark bycatch was significantly greater in June-August than September-October. The odds of observing shark bycatch during April-May was also significantly different from September-October. However, these differences were only apparent east of 93 degrees W (central Louisiana). For the 1994 and 1995 fishing seasons we estimated an annual take of approximately 30,000 sharks. Stomach analyses on sharks indicated that the menhaden schools were functioning as a foraging base for those sharks captured. While detailed age and growth information were not collected, comparisons to length distributions in the literature indicated that the fishery appears to be impacting the summer nursery grounds of sharks in the northern Gulf of Mexico.

abstract_text: We studied the density-dependent aspects of growth, development, and survivorship of arboreal tadpoles of Chirixalus eiffingeri in bamboo forests at the Experimental Forest of the National Taiwan University at Chitou, Taiwan, from May-September 1995. Newly hatched tadpoles were randomly assigned to one of the three treatments: low (LD), medium (MD), and high density (HD) (six, 18, and 54 tadpoles/bamboo stump, respectively), and each treatment consisted of 15 replicates. Tadpoles are obligatorily oophagous; thus, growth, development, and survivorship of tadpoles are totally dependent upon trophic egg availability. Tadpoles in all treatments increased in mass during development, but LD and MD tadpoles grew faster and weighed significantly heavier than HD tadpoles by week 5. During the first 5 weeks of development, the biomass increase of tadpoles (BMI) in successful nests was substantially greater than zero and was significantly different between treatments, indicating that female frogs are capable of increasing the supply of trophic eggs as the tadpole number increased in MD and HD treatments. Body size at metamorphosis was density-dependent but the time required to reach metamorphosis was not, which was different from earlier studies on pond breeders. This discrepancy is probably due to the different feeding habits (i.e., herbivory versus oophagy) and size-selective feeding behavior. Results suggest that the energetic reserves of female frogs for brooding strongly affect the growth, development, and survivorship of tadpoles.

title: Contributions to the life history of the redback salamander: preliminary evidence for kin recognition

abstract_text: We tested two questions critical to the reproductive life history of the redback salamander (Plethodon cinereus): (1) Do females recognize and preferentially brood their own eggs during pair-wise discrimination trials? (2) Are hatchlings able to recognize their mother using substrate-borne chemical cues, and if so, is this ability innate or learned? To address the first question, we tested brooding females collected from the field within a few days of oviposition. They were given a choice of their own eggs and those of a conspecific female, and their association monitored over a 24 h period. To address the second question we collected 60 females within 24 h post-oviposition, and divided them into two groups. The eggs of group 1 were raised by their mothers until they hatched. The eggs of group 2 were isolated on filter paper throughout development. Beginning at 2 weeks post-hatching, each juvenile was tested twice (24 h each) in pair-wise trials contrasting unmarked filter paper with filter paper scented with maternal odors. Our results confirm maternal egg recognition in P. cinereus, and we present preliminary data suggesting that juveniles chemically imprint on their mother during the prolonged maternal brooding period.

title: Reproductive success in the bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana

abstract_text: We studied mating behavior and reproductive success in a wild, northern population of bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana). The predominant selective mechanism in this system was female choice. Male bullfrogs gathered annually at traditional chorusing sites where they competed aggressively or employed alternate mating strategies in an attempt to acquire mates. Females entered the choruses briefly to select a mate, engage in amplexus, and deposit eggs. Compared with males that were unsuccessful in obtaining mates, reproductively successful males were larger, had longer tenures in the choruses, spent more of their tenure calling, and had previous chorusing experience. Male size was related to reproductive effort with larger males losing proportionately more weight over the chorusing season. In females, clutch volume was positively related to body size with large females depositing egg masses up to three times larger than those of small females. There was no evidence of assortative mating by body size. We also postulated that, because of a low population density, this system may best be described as a lek in contrast to the resource-defense system described previously for this species.
